Machine learning for chemistry
Teaching a neural network the O–O bond
Neural-network potential energy surfaces, from a single neuron to forces and vibrational frequencies
Jonathan M. Smith · Temple University | Slides and worked example built in collaboration with Claude (Anthropic)
The problem
A potential energy surface is expensive to compute and needed everywhere
Quantum chemistry is slow
One energy at one geometry: minutes to days.
Dynamics needs millions of calls
MD needs V and F = −dV/dr at every time step.
So learn V from a few samples
Fit a fast, smooth V(r); differentiate for forces.
Our test case: O₂
V(r) = Dₑ[1 − exp(−a(r − rₑ))]² − Dₑ
Parameter
Value
Well depth Dₑ
5.21 eV
Bond length rₑ
1.208 Å
Width a
2.66 Å⁻¹
Training points
36, 0.95–3.0 Å
A Morse curve stands in for quantum-chemistry data, so we know the right answer.
The model
Inside the network: weigh, add, then bend
One neuron
z = w·x + b (weigh and add) a = GELU(z) = z·Φ(z) (bend)
━ GELU: smooth everywhere
╌ ReLU: sharp corner at 0
The network
Input: bond length r (standardized)
Hidden layer 1: 16 GELU neurons
Hidden layer 2: 16 GELU neurons
Output: V(r) in eV (linear)
Why GELU for a PES? Forces are −dV/dr and frequencies need d²V/dr². GELU keeps both smooth; ReLU gives a piecewise-linear V with jumping forces.
Training, live
Watch the network learn the O–O curve
━ network ● data ╌ Morse ━ neuron pieces
Pieces add up. Each green curve is one last-layer neuron times its weight; their sum is the blue curve.
Wall first, tail last. Big errors at the repulsive wall get fixed first; the flat dissociation tail is where pieces must cancel.
8 neurons per layer, trained in your browser with plain JavaScript and Adam.
The loss and the optimizer
Training: what we minimize, and how
Spikes mean the steps are too big. Cutting the learning rate at epoch 2,000 lets training settle into the minimum.
L = mean[(V − Vref)²] + λ · mean[(F − Fref)²]
Mean squared error on energies and forces, with λ = 0.1 Å² balancing the two.
  1. Forward: predict V and F = −dV/dr at all 36 points
  2. Loss: score both against the reference
  3. Backprop: the chain rule gives ∂L/∂w for all 321 weights
  4. Adam: each weight takes its own adaptive step

Why one autograd call is enough
Each Vᵢ depends only on its own rᵢ, so the gradient of ΣVᵢ gives every dVᵢ/drᵢ at once.
Full batch vs. mini-batch
36 points fit in one batch. Large data sets use a random mini-batch per step (stochastic gradient descent).
The code, annotated
Training and reading out in PyTorch
① Train: 36 points per step
r = R.reshape(-1, 1)            # (36,1): all points at once model = PES()                   # 1→16→16→1 GELU + scaling opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01) for epoch in range(6000):     opt.zero_grad()             # clear last step’s gradients     r.requires_grad_(True)      # track r so we can take dV/dr     V = model(r)                # (36,1) energies     dVdr, = torch.autograd.grad(V.sum(), r,                                 create_graph=True)     F = -dVdr                   # (36,1) forces     loss = ((V - V_ref)**2).mean() \          + 0.1 * ((F - F_ref)**2).mean()  # 1 number     loss.backward()             # ∂loss/∂w for all 321 weights     opt.step()                  # one Adam update
② Read out: any grid, no loop
model.eval() r = torch.linspace(0.9, 3.1, 400) r = r.reshape(-1, 1)  # (400,1) r.requires_grad_(True) V = model(r)          # (400,1) dVdr, = torch.autograd.grad(             V.sum(), r) F = -dVdr             # (400,1)

Inside the trained model
The fitted O–O network, color-coded
321
learned numbers: 288 weights and 33 biases
Lines are weights: red +, blue −, thicker = larger. Circles are colored by each neuron’s bias.
The first layer sets where each neuron bends along r; the output layer mixes signs so pieces add up at the wall and cancel in the flat tail.
No single neuron “is” the bond: the curve is spread across all the weights.
Same network, different activation
Why GELU suits molecular surfaces and their gradients
Smooth gradient → real forces
ReLU’s derivative is a step, so forces jump. Force error: 1.5 vs 0.023 eV/Å.
Curvature exists → spectroscopy
ReLU’s d²V/dr² is zero almost everywhere: no ωₑ. GELU gives ≈ 1580 cm⁻¹.
No saturation → trains well
Unlike tanh, GELU passes large inputs, keeping gradients alive in deep nets.
Beyond the training range
Outside the data: confident and wrong
Not random, just unconstrained
Far from data, GELU nets become straight lines. At 0.3 Å: 35–56 eV vs. 536 eV.
Disagreement flags danger
Seeds agree to 0.00 eV inside the data, but differ by 23 eV at 10 Å.
The fixes
Sample where you simulate, build physics in, and flag out-of-range inputs.
Physics in the architecture
Build the physics in: V(∞) = 0 by design
y = exp(−(r − rₑ)/λ) V(r) = g(y) − g(0)
As r → ∞, y → 0, so V → g(0) − g(0) = 0 exactly.
